questions.stem: The nurse is preparing a single injection of regular insulin 6 units and NPH insulin 14 units. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Inject 14 units of air into the NPH vial without withdrawing insulin
Withdraw 14 units of NPH insulin into the same syringe, for a total of 20 units
Inject 6 units of air into the regular insulin vial

rationale.correct: Air into cloudy, air into clear, draw clear, then draw cloudy. This keeps intermediate-acting insulin out of the regular insulin vial.

perOption.a: Air goes into the cloudy (NPH) vial first, so the needle never touches NPH before drawing regular insulin.
perOption.b: Adding air to the regular vial makes withdrawal easier.
perOption.c: Clear (regular) insulin is drawn up first so it isn't contaminated with NPH.
perOption.d: Cloudy insulin is drawn last.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Mix regular and NPH insulin in one syringe correctly.

questions.stem: A client receives NPH insulin at 0700. When is the client at greatest risk for hypoglycemia?

options.text: Late morning to late afternoon
Bedtime
The next morning before breakfast

rationale.correct: Hypoglycemia is most likely during an insulin's peak; NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after injection.

perOption.a: NPH begins working 1 to 2 hours after injection, so it isn't yet active.
perOption.b: NPH peaks about 4 to 12 hours after injection.
perOption.c: By bedtime the peak effect of a morning NPH dose is wearing off.
perOption.d: NPH lasts about 18 to 24 hours, and its peak is long past.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Link insulin peak times to hypoglycemia risk.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who has started insulin glargine at bedtime. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take it at the same time every day."
"I'll mix it with my rapid-acting insulin to save an injection."
"It works all day and doesn't have a strong peak."
"I'll keep checking my blood sugar as instructed."

rationale.correct: Long-acting insulin analogs such as glargine and detemir are never mixed with other insulins.

perOption.a: Consistent timing keeps basal insulin levels steady.
perOption.b: Glargine must not be mixed with other insulins because mixing changes how it is absorbed.
perOption.c: Glargine is a long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak.
perOption.d: Monitoring is still essential.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach safe use of long-acting insulin.

questions.stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis needs a continuous IV insulin infusion. Which insulin should the nurse expect to use?

options.text: Regular insulin
NPH insulin
Insulin glargine
Insulin detemir

rationale.correct: Regular insulin is the standard insulin for IV infusion.

perOption.a: Regular (short-acting) insulin is the insulin routinely given IV.
perOption.b: NPH is a suspension and must never be given IV.
perOption.c: Glargine is given subcutaneously only.
perOption.d: Detemir is given subcutaneously only.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the insulin used for IV infusion.

questions.stem: A client who weighs 70 kg is prescribed an insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr. The bag contains 100 units of regular insulin in 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride. At what rate should the nurse set the pump?

rationale.correct: Dose: 0.1 units/kg/hr × 70 kg = 7 units/hr. Concentration: 100 units ÷ 100 mL = 1 unit/mL. Rate: 7 units/hr ÷ 1 unit/mL = 7 mL/hr.
references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes is due for prescribed insulin lispro with lunch. The client's glucose is 52 mg/dL and the client is alert. Complete the sentence.

content.template: The nurse should {{b1}} the scheduled lispro and first {{b2}}.

options.text: hold
give
double
give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
give 1 mg of glucagon IM
give a high-fat snack such as peanut butter

rationale.correct: Treat hypoglycemia before giving rapid-acting insulin, and contact the provider about adjusting the dose.

perOption.b1:a: Giving rapid-acting insulin with a glucose of 52 mg/dL would deepen the hypoglycemia.
perOption.b1:b: Lispro lowers glucose within 15 minutes and would make the hypoglycemia worse.
perOption.b1:c: Increasing insulin is dangerous with hypoglycemia.
perOption.b2:a: The 15-15 rule treats mild to moderate hypoglycemia in an alert client.
perOption.b2:b: Glucagon is for clients who can't swallow safely.
perOption.b2:c: Fat slows the absorption of glucose.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to hypoglycemia before giving mealtime insulin.

questions.stem: A client using a morphine PCA pump after surgery is hard to rouse and has a respiratory rate of 7/min and an oxygen saturation of 86%. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Document the findings and reassess in 15 minutes
Stop the PCA, try to rouse the client and prepare to give naloxone per protocol
Lower the PCA dose and let the client continue to use it
Tell the client's family to stop pressing the PCA button

rationale.correct: Excessive sedation comes before respiratory depression. Stop the opioid, stimulate the client, support breathing and give naloxone.

perOption.a: This is respiratory depression and needs action now.
perOption.b: Stopping the opioid, stimulating the client and reversing with naloxone treats opioid-induced respiratory depression.
perOption.c: Any further opioid could worsen the respiratory depression.
perOption.d: This may help prevent future problems but doesn't treat the current emergency.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to opioid-induced respiratory depression.

questions.stem: The nurse gave IV naloxone to a client with opioid-induced respiratory depression. The client is now awake with a respiratory rate of 14/min. Why must the nurse keep monitoring the client closely?

options.text: Naloxone often causes hypoglycemia
Naloxone's effect may wear off before the opioid's, so respiratory depression can return
Naloxone can cause respiratory depression on its own
The client will need a higher opioid dose immediately

rationale.correct: Because naloxone has a short half-life, monitor for re-sedation and watch for withdrawal and pain.

perOption.a: Hypoglycemia isn't a typical effect of naloxone.
perOption.b: Naloxone lasts about 30 to 90 minutes, shorter than many opioids, so repeat doses may be needed.
perOption.c: Naloxone reverses respiratory depression.
perOption.d: Pain management must be adjusted carefully, not increased immediately.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Monitor for recurrent sedation after naloxone.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is going home with oxycodone for pain. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Increase fluid and fiber intake and use a stool softener as prescribed
Avoid alcohol and other sedatives
Don't drive until you know how the medication affects you
Store the medication in a locked place
Crush extended-release tablets if they are hard to swallow
Take an extra dose if the pain is not relieved

rationale.correct: Opioid teaching covers constipation, sedation safety, avoiding other depressants, safe storage and never altering extended-release forms.

perOption.a: Opioids slow the bowel, and constipation doesn't improve with time.
perOption.b: Combining depressants increases the risk of respiratory depression.
perOption.c: Opioids cause drowsiness and slow reactions.
perOption.d: Secure storage prevents misuse by others.
perOption.e: Crushing extended-release tablets releases the whole dose at once and can be fatal.
perOption.f: Extra doses increase the risk of overdose; the client should contact the provider instead.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach safe opioid use at home.

questions.stem: A client has been prescribed a transdermal fentanyl patch. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take off the old patch before putting on a new one."
"I'll put a heating pad over the patch when my back hurts."
"I'll fold the used patch with the sticky sides together before throwing it away."
"I'll put each new patch on a different area of skin."

rationale.correct: Heat (heating pads, hot tubs, fever) speeds up fentanyl absorption and can cause dangerous toxicity.

perOption.a: Removing the old patch prevents overdose.
perOption.b: Heat increases fentanyl absorption and can cause overdose.
perOption.c: Folding the patch prevents accidental exposure.
perOption.d: Rotating sites prevents skin irritation.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Before starting an IV infusion of potassium chloride, which assessment is most important?

options.text: Urine output
Temperature
Blood glucose
Respiratory rate

rationale.correct: Check kidney function before IV potassium. Never give it IV push, and always dilute it and use an infusion pump.

perOption.a: Potassium is excreted by the kidneys; urine output of at least 30 mL/hr is needed to avoid hyperkalemia.
perOption.b: Temperature doesn't affect potassium safety.
perOption.c: Glucose isn't the main safety check before potassium.
perOption.d: Respiratory rate isn't the main safety check before potassium.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Assess kidney function before giving IV potassium.

questions.stem: The nurse observes a student giving enoxaparin from a prefilled syringe. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Chooses a site on the abdomen at least 5 cm (2 inches) from the navel
Leaves the air bubble in the prefilled syringe
Rubs the injection site after giving the medication
Inserts the needle at a 90-degree angle into a pinched skin fold

rationale.correct: Don't expel the air bubble from the prefilled syringe, don't aspirate and don't rub the site after giving enoxaparin.

perOption.a: This is the correct site for enoxaparin.
perOption.b: The bubble is left in so the full dose is given.
perOption.c: Rubbing increases bruising and hematoma formation.
perOption.d: This is the correct technique.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Give low-molecular-weight heparin correctly.

questions.stem: For each drug causing toxicity, select the antidote or reversal agent.

options.text: Protamine sulfate
Vitamin K
Naloxone
Flumazenil
Protamine sulfate
Vitamin K
Acetylcysteine
Digoxin immune fab
Naloxone
Flumazenil
Atropine
Protamine sulfate
Naloxone
Flumazenil
Vitamin K
Glucagon
Acetylcysteine
Naloxone
Deferoxamine
Protamine sulfate

rationale.correct: Know the common antidotes: protamine (heparin), vitamin K (warfarin), naloxone (opioids), flumazenil (benzodiazepines), acetylcysteine (acetaminophen), digoxin immune fab (digoxin).

perOption.b1:a: Protamine binds heparin and neutralizes it.
perOption.b2:b: Vitamin K restores the clotting factors warfarin blocks.
perOption.b3:c: Atropine treats bradycardia and cholinergic toxicity.
perOption.b4:d: Glucagon treats hypoglycemia and beta-blocker toxicity.
perOption.b5:a: Acetylcysteine restores glutathione and protects the liver.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Match drugs to their antidotes.

questions.stem: A client taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 5.2 and no signs of bleeding. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the scheduled warfarin dose
Hold the warfarin and notify the provider
Give protamine sulfate
Double the next day's dose

rationale.correct: Hold warfarin for a supratherapeutic INR and notify the provider; the target INR for atrial fibrillation is 2 to 3.

perOption.a: Giving more warfarin with a high INR raises the risk of bleeding.
perOption.b: The INR is above the 2 to 3 target; the dose is held and the provider decides on further action, such as vitamin K.
perOption.c: Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.
perOption.d: This would raise the INR further.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a high INR in a client taking warfarin.

questions.stem: A client starting apixaban for atrial fibrillation asks, "How often will I need my INR checked?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Every week for the first month."
"Routine INR monitoring isn't needed with this medication."
"Monthly, like warfarin."
"Only if you eat a lot of leafy green vegetables."

rationale.correct: DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) don't need routine INR monitoring. Clients still need bleeding precautions and periodic kidney function tests.

perOption.a: INR monitoring isn't used for apixaban.
perOption.b: Direct oral anticoagulants such as apixaban have predictable effects and don't need routine INR checks.
perOption.c: INR is used to monitor warfarin, not apixaban.
perOption.d: Vitamin K intake affects warfarin, not apixaban.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach a client about monitoring direct oral anticoagulants.

questions.stem: A client with an acute ischemic stroke is being evaluated for IV alteplase. Which finding makes alteplase contraindicated?

options.text: Symptoms started 2 hours ago
Platelet count of 80,000/mm3
Age of 72
Blood glucose of 110 mg/dL

rationale.correct: Before giving a thrombolytic, check for bleeding risks: low platelets, recent surgery or bleeding, uncontrolled hypertension (above 185/110) and intracranial hemorrhage.

perOption.a: Alteplase is given within 3 to 4.5 hours of symptom onset.
perOption.b: A platelet count below 100,000/mm3 raises the risk of bleeding and is a contraindication.
perOption.c: Age alone isn't a contraindication within the 3-hour window.
perOption.d: This glucose is acceptable; very low glucose can mimic a stroke and is checked first.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify contraindications to thrombolytic therapy.

questions.stem: A client receiving IV gentamicin reports ringing in the ears. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client this is an expected, harmless effect
Hold the next dose and notify the provider
Give the dose with food
Increase the infusion rate

rationale.correct: Aminoglycosides can cause ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Monitor hearing, balance, creatinine and drug levels.

perOption.a: Tinnitus is a sign of ototoxicity, which can become permanent.
perOption.b: Ototoxicity is a serious adverse effect of aminoglycosides; the provider may change the drug or the dose.
perOption.c: Food doesn't affect IV gentamicin or its ototoxicity.
perOption.d: A faster infusion increases peak levels and toxicity.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize aminoglycoside ototoxicity.

questions.stem: Ten minutes after a unit of packed red blood cells is started, the client reports chills and low back pain. The temperature has risen 1.5 °C. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Slow the transfusion and recheck vital signs in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion and keep the IV open with 0.9% sodium chloride through new tubing
Give acetaminophen and continue the transfusion
Take the blood bag back to the blood bank

rationale.correct: For any suspected transfusion reaction: stop the transfusion, keep the vein open with saline through new tubing, notify the provider and the blood bank, and monitor the client.

perOption.a: Slowing a possible hemolytic reaction lets more incompatible blood in.
perOption.b: Stopping the blood limits the reaction, and new tubing avoids giving the blood left in the line.
perOption.c: Treating symptoms without stopping the transfusion may be fatal in an acute hemolytic reaction.
perOption.d: The bag and tubing are returned, but only after the client is safe.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a suspected transfusion reaction.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give a unit of packed red blood cells. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check the client and unit identification with another licensed nurse at the bedside
Prime the tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride
Use blood tubing with a filter
Stay with the client for the first 15 minutes
Prime the tubing with D5W
Warm the blood in a microwave to prevent hypothermia

rationale.correct: Safe transfusion: verified identity, normal saline only, filtered tubing, close early monitoring and completion within 4 hours.

perOption.a: A two-person bedside check prevents ABO-incompatible transfusions.
perOption.b: Only normal saline is compatible with blood.
perOption.c: A filter removes clots and debris.
perOption.d: Most severe reactions happen early.
perOption.e: Dextrose solutions cause red blood cells to clump and hemolyze.
perOption.f: Microwaving damages cells; an approved blood warmer is used if needed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prepare to give a blood transfusion safely.

questions.stem: A client's bag of total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is empty and the pharmacy says the next bag will be 2 hours late. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Flush the line and leave it capped until the new bag arrives
Hang 10% dextrose in water at the TPN rate
Hang 0.9% sodium chloride at the TPN rate
Speed up the next bag when it arrives to make up the missed volume

rationale.correct: Hang D10W if TPN is interrupted, and never speed up TPN to catch up. Monitor glucose closely.

perOption.a: Stopping TPN suddenly can cause rebound hypoglycemia.
perOption.b: D10W maintains glucose delivery and prevents rebound hypoglycemia.
perOption.c: Saline doesn't provide glucose.
perOption.d: Catching up can cause hyperglycemia and fluid overload.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent hypoglycemia when TPN is interrupted.

questions.stem: A client's central venous catheter tubing comes apart during a position change. The client suddenly becomes short of breath with chest pain. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Clamp the catheter
Place the client flat on the back
Give oxygen
Call the provider

rationale.correct: For suspected air embolism: clamp the catheter, put the client on the left side with the head down (if not contraindicated), give oxygen and notify the provider.

perOption.a: Clamping stops more air from entering the circulation.
perOption.b: The left-side, head-down position is used after the catheter is clamped.
perOption.c: Oxygen is needed, but stopping more air from entering comes first.
perOption.d: The provider is notified after immediate actions.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a suspected air embolism from a central line.

questions.stem: A client's peripheral IV site is cool, pale and swollen, and the infusion has slowed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter and elevate the arm
Flush the catheter forcefully to clear it
Apply a warm compress and continue the infusion
Raise the IV bag higher to improve flow

rationale.correct: Infiltration is cool, pale and swollen; phlebitis is warm, red and tender along the vein.

perOption.a: These findings indicate infiltration; the IV is stopped and removed and the arm elevated.
perOption.b: Forceful flushing pushes more fluid into the tissue.
perOption.c: The infusion must be stopped first.
perOption.d: This forces more fluid into the tissue.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize and manage IV infiltration.

questions.stem: A client receiving norepinephrine through a peripheral IV has a cold, blanched area around the insertion site. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Stop the infusion and notify the provider so phentolamine can be given into the area
Apply ice to the site and continue the infusion
Increase the infusion rate to maintain blood pressure
Massage the area to spread the medication

rationale.correct: Vasopressor extravasation is treated by stopping the infusion and giving phentolamine; vasopressors are preferably given through a central line.

perOption.a: Norepinephrine extravasation causes vasoconstriction and tissue necrosis; phentolamine reverses the local vasoconstriction.
perOption.b: Ice worsens vasoconstriction, and the infusion must be stopped at that site.
perOption.c: This increases tissue damage.
perOption.d: Massage spreads the drug and the damage.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage extravasation of a vasopressor.

questions.stem: The nurse is giving an intramuscular injection of iron dextran. Which technique should the nurse use?

options.text: Z-track method
Massaging the site after injection
Injecting into the deltoid muscle
Using the same needle used to draw up the drug

rationale.correct: Z-track injection prevents irritating or staining drugs from leaking into subcutaneous tissue.

perOption.a: The Z-track method seals the medication in the muscle, preventing leakage and skin staining.
perOption.b: Massage can push the drug into the subcutaneous tissue and stain the skin.
perOption.c: A large muscle such as the ventrogluteal is preferred.
perOption.d: A new needle prevents tracking the irritating drug through the tissue.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Use the Z-track method for irritating IM medications.

questions.stem: The nurse is giving furosemide 80 mg by IV push. Which action helps prevent ototoxicity?

options.text: Give the dose over at least 4 minutes (no faster than 20 mg/min)
Give the dose with a glass of milk
Give the dose as quickly as possible
Give it into the IM site instead

rationale.correct: Give IV furosemide slowly, at no more than about 20 mg/min; the risk of ototoxicity rises with fast or high doses.

perOption.a: Rapid IV push of high-dose furosemide raises the risk of ototoxicity.
perOption.b: Food doesn't affect IV furosemide.
perOption.c: Rapid administration increases the risk of hearing damage.
perOption.d: Changing the route without an order isn't appropriate.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Give IV push furosemide at a safe rate.

questions.stem: Select the 3 assessments the nurse should check before giving these medications.

options.text: Blood pressure before giving lisinopril
Apical pulse for 1 full minute before giving digoxin
Potassium level before giving IV furosemide
Temperature before giving metoprolol
Blood glucose before giving amlodipine
Respiratory rate before giving atorvastatin

rationale.correct: Before giving cardiovascular drugs, check the vital sign or lab value the drug affects.

perOption.a: Lisinopril lowers blood pressure; hold it if the client is hypotensive.
perOption.b: Hold digoxin for a heart rate below 60/min (or per the prescriber's parameters).
perOption.c: Furosemide wastes potassium; hypokalemia must be corrected first.
perOption.d: Metoprolol needs a heart rate and blood pressure check.
perOption.e: Amlodipine needs a blood pressure check.
perOption.f: Statins need monitoring of liver function and muscle symptoms.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.
